"I Wish There Was a Treaty We Could Sign":
An Inquiry into the Making of the Global Pact
for the Environment
MARIE-CATHERINE PETERSMANN*
ABSTRACT
This article provides ethnographic insights into the making of the latest
UN-backed instrument for transnational environmental law and
governance: the Global Pact for the Environment (GPE). It narrates the
rise and fall of a contemporary policy project designed to unify and
strengthen international environmental law. The story starts in 2015 on
the premises of a Parisian legal think tank and ends in May 2019 at the
headquarters of the United Nations Environment Programme in
Nairobi, where states ultimately decided not to adopt the GPE as a
legally binding instrument but opted to prepare apolitical declaration to
be presented in 2022 at the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the UN
Conference on the Human Environment. The time between 2015 and
2019 is divided in two periods. From 2015 to 2017, the GPE was
imagined, drafted, and promoted by a group of non-state actors mainly

of primary sources, the article traces the multiplicity of actants enrolled
in the GPE, the interests that held them together, and the institutional

to reassemble the bonds between human

questioning the politics of policy-entrepreneurship and consensus-
building the tenuous and fragile modes of existence that mark
contemporary international law.
INTRODUCTION
Over 
the 
past 
years, 
scholarly 
debates 
in 
international
environmental law (IEL) have been animated by lively discussions on
the 
overarching 
structure, 
normative 
architecture, 
and future
orientation of the field in light of the possible adoption of a Global Pact
for the Environment (GPE).1 While extensively commented upon in the
literature, the GPE remains a mystical creature born through the
interactional work of scholars, practitioners, think tanks, corporations,
NGOs, international organizations (IOs), state officials, and public
figures who mobilized or were mobilized for the initiative. This article is
not directly interested in the conceptual regulatory framework
established in the preliminary text of the GPE, which has been subject
to considerable scrutiny from international legal scholars. 2 It adopts,
instead, an ethnographic perspective that retraces the distinct
communities of practice that have been enrolled and mobilized in the
process, the formation and circulation of shared interests, the material
and discursive 
articulations legitimizing the initiative, 
and the
moments of institutional translation that stabilized and destabilized the
making of the GPE-from its initial stages to the current state of

environmental lawmaking in the contemporary conjuncture of global
governance.
Methodologically, the descriptive, nonessentialist, and ethnographic
nature of the inquiry is inspired by Bruno Latour's actor-network theory
(ANT), and the material semiotic method he pioneered-with John Law
and Michel Callon-to map relations that are simultaneously material
(between things) and semiotic (between concepts). 4 This approach is
particularly productive to study the composite processes, norms, and
objects that co-produce contemporary policy instruments, such as the
GPE. A complex web of state and non-state actors, institutional
procedures, 
UN 
resolutions 
and 
declarations, 
and 
political
endorsements are assembled behind the initiative, which the article
aims to unpack. To reveal the role played by human and nonhuman
actants that weave this multifaceted network together, the article
retrieves the relational and agential dynamics of the GPE by drawing
on Callon's "four moments of translation." 5 In the first phase,

problematization, a primary actor identifies a problem and pinpoints
what actors are required within a network to address this problem and
its related knowledge claim. 6 The second phase, interessement, begins
when the primary actor starts building the actor-network by negotiating
with other actors regarding the roles they may play within the network
and the achievements they promise to reach when joining it.7 The third
phase, enrolment, characterizes the time following those negotiations,
when actors accept (or reject) the roles they have been asked to perform
and become part of this network of alliances. 8 Finally, the mobilization
phase occurs when allies external to the network support it.9 Once
established, a robust apparatus of maintenance and stabilization of the
heterogenous network is put in place, to render it durable and address
ongoing resistance and struggles among internal and against external
actors. The translations of these counterstrategies and compromises
continuously readjust the network, in line with its reconfigured web of
associations, enrolments, and counter-enrolments. 10
This analysis is based on archival research and fieldwork conducted
to describe and understand the formation, agenda, and practices of the
International Group of Experts for the Pact (IGEP), semi-structured
interviews with actors involved in the GPE initiative, and participant
observation during the meetings they held. The adopted socio-legal and
ethnographic approach sheds light on the relations between actants,
concepts, discourses, documents, institutions, and objects that translate
and bind the GPE together. In doing so, the analysis highlights the
promises of an instrument meant to act as a pivot in unifying the
fragmented legal obligations scattered across the field and sub-regimes
of IEL. Simultaneously, it also unveils the fixed formats and socio-
technical channels that constrain such initiatives through patterns of
institutional path dependence and, ultimately, inertia. The story
thereby narrates the rise and fall of a contemporary project of
transnational environmental lawmaking. What comes to light is how
grand political aspirations and normative ideals of law are generated,
mediated, and sterilized by their passage through a particular

CONCLUSION
This article recounted how the GPE emerged and evolved as an
artefact of international legal thought and practice: where and why it
originated, how it expanded and circulated with the enrolment of new
actants over time, and how this affected its translation into an adaptive
and fragile material-semiotic network. 415 From its inception in the
Parisian legal think tank CDJ in 2015, to the French Constitutional
Council in 2017, the UNGA in New York in 2018, UN Environment in
Nairobi in 2019, and its latest translation into a political declaration to
be adopted at the Stockholm+50 Earth Summit in June 2022, this
instrument is in perpetual motion. Both its format and its scope are
reflexively shaped and transformed by every new translation it
undergoes. With each enrolment and counter-enrolment, every failure
and risk of unravelment that needed to be managed, the network of
